title: Sneaker reseller (NOOK Dunk Low): FIFO cost of goods sold and gross profit, and comparing the four inventory valuation methods
participant_role: Entrepreneur and accounting student who runs a sneaker resale business and has calculated cost of goods sold on the NOOK Dunk Low
judge_role: Tax accountant meeting the entrepreneur to review cost of goods sold and inventory valuation methods
scenario:
You are to assume the role of an entrepreneur that is also an accounting student. Your tax accountant (judge) will be meeting with you to discuss your cost of goods sold and inventory valuation methods.

You have started your own business as a sneaker reseller who buys sneakers and attempts to sell them for a profit. You are getting ready to meet with your tax accountant (judge) to discuss the cost of goods sold. Since you have been studying accounting, you have decided to calculate this yourself. You are familiar with the four methods of valuing inventory: specific identification, First-in, First-out (FIFO), Last-in, First-out (LIFO) and weighted averages.

You have decided to do the calculation on only the transactions related to the popular NOOK brand Dunk Low sneaker. You want to verify understanding of the process with the tax accountant (judge).

The NOOK Dunk Low sneaker was launched on the NOOK SNKRS app in early June. There was immense hype with sneaker fans for this product launch. Therefore, you felt that the shoe would quickly increase in value and be a profitable investment.

You will use the following transactions to calculate cost of goods sold and gross profit using FIFO:

June 3rd: You win the draw for the shoe on the NOOK SNKRS app and purchase it for retail at $100.
June 5th: A friend also wins the draw on the NOOK SNKRS app and you buy their pair for $180.
June 7th: You purchase four pairs of the shoe from SNEAKER KICKS CO. for $210 each.
June 13th: You purchase 2 more pairs of the shoe from another reseller at SNEAKERCON for $250 each.
June 21st: You sell 3 pairs of the shoe for $270 each.

You will meet with the tax accountant (judge) to discuss the following:
- Review the calculations
- Verify understanding of the four inventory valuation methods
- Explain which method will generate the lowest gross profit based on the transactions above in which the costs are rising

You will present the information to the tax accountant (judge) in a role-play to take place in the tax accountant's (judge's) office. The tax accountant (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the tax accountant's (judge's) questions, the tax accountant (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Why is it important to calculate cost of goods sold?
When is it appropriate to use Last in First out (LIFO)?

solution.overview: A strong answer walks through FIFO: the 3 pairs sold on June 21 are costed at the three oldest purchases ($100 + $180 + $210 = $490), so gross profit is $810 minus $490 = $320 and the remaining 5 pairs (3 at $210 and 2 at $250, $1,130) stay in inventory. The presenter then defines specific identification, FIFO, LIFO and weighted average, and concludes that with rising costs LIFO gives the lowest gross profit ($100 here) because the newest, most expensive pairs go into cost of goods sold.

by_task.task: FIFO cost of goods sold and gross profit
answer: 8 pairs were bought for a total of $1,620 (100 + 180 + 840 + 500)
FIFO sells the oldest pairs first: June 3 pair $100, June 5 pair $180, one June 7 pair $210
Cost of goods sold = $100 + $180 + $210 = $490
Sales = 3 x $270 = $810; gross profit = $810 minus $490 = $320
Ending inventory = 3 pairs at $210 + 2 pairs at $250 = $1,130 (check: $1,620 minus $490)
Specific identification: used for high-cost, low-volume items; COGS is the actual cost of the exact pairs sold (workable for sneakers if each pair is tracked by receipt)
FIFO: the most used method; COGS uses the older purchases and ending inventory is made up of the newer purchases
LIFO: COGS uses the newest purchases and ending inventory is made up of the older purchases
Weighted average: one average cost per unit ($1,620 / 8 = $202.50) is used for both COGS and ending inventory
All four are cost-flow assumptions; the physical pair handed to the buyer can be any of them (except under specific identification)

by_task.task: Which method gives the lowest gross profit when costs are rising
answer: LIFO, because the most recent (highest) purchase costs make up cost of goods sold
LIFO here: 2 x $250 + 1 x $210 = $710 COGS, gross profit $810 minus $710 = $100
Compare: FIFO gross profit $320, weighted average $202.50 (COGS 3 x $202.50 = $607.50), LIFO $100
Lower gross profit means lower taxable income, which is why a tax accountant cares about the method choice
Whatever method is chosen must be used consistently from year to year

judge_question_answers.question: Why is it important to calculate cost of goods sold?
answer: COGS is subtracted from sales to find gross profit, the first measure of whether the resale business actually makes money
It determines taxable income, so it must be calculated correctly and consistently for the tax return
It shows the true profit per pair, which guides what price to pay for future sneakers and what price to sell at
It also sets the value of ending inventory reported on the balance sheet

judge_question_answers.question: When is it appropriate to use Last in First out (LIFO)?
answer: When costs are rising and the business wants to match current (higher) costs against current sales, which lowers reported profit and taxes
For goods that are not perishable and where the physical flow does not matter, such as bulk materials or, here, identical sneakers
Only where it is allowed: US GAAP and the IRS permit LIFO (with a conformity rule that it be used for both books and taxes), but IFRS does not
Not appropriate when costs are falling, when inventory turns over very quickly, or when the physical flow is clearly first-in first-out

key_concepts.definition: The cost of the inventory actually sold during the period. Under a cost-flow method, COGS = Units sold x Cost assigned to those units.
Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold; the profit before operating expenses and taxes.
Assumes the oldest costs are sold first, so COGS is made of older purchases and ending inventory of newer purchases. In rising-cost periods it gives the highest gross profit.
Assumes the newest costs are sold first, so COGS is made of the most recent purchases. In rising-cost periods it gives the lowest gross profit and lowest taxes.
Assigns every unit the same average cost: Total cost of goods available / Total units available. Here $1,620 / 8 = $202.50 per pair.
Tracks the actual cost of each individual item sold; practical for high-cost, low-volume goods like cars, jewelry or collectible sneakers.

key_concepts.term: Cost of goods available for sale
key_concepts.definition: Beginning inventory + Purchases during the period; it is split between COGS and ending inventory.
Cost of goods available minus COGS; the value of unsold units carried on the balance sheet as a current asset.
An accounting choice about which costs are assigned to sold units; it does not have to match which physical pair the customer received.
A business should apply the same inventory method every period so results are comparable; a change must be justified and disclosed.
US tax rule that a business using LIFO for its tax return must also use LIFO in its financial statements.
